t: Check if Word Equals Summation of Two Words — Words as Decimal Numerals
o: Letters a through j double as digits 0 through 9, so any word over this alphabet reads as a decimal numeral: acb becomes 021, interpreted as 21. The task reduces to checking num(firstWord) + num(secondWord) == num(targetWord). Example 1: acb -> 21, cba -> 210, cdb -> 231, and indeed 21 + 210 == 231, so we return true. Example 2: aaa -> 000 -> 0 twice against aaaa -> 0123 -> 123, and 0 + 0 != 123, hence false. Words run at most 8 letters, values stay below 10^8, and the leading zeros produced by letter a vanish under any numeric interpretation — every correct method here is instant.
k: The alphabet a-j maps exactly onto decimal digits 0-9, making a word literally a numeral.
Horner-style accumulation v = v * 10 + digit parses a word in one allocation-free pass.
Leading zeros from letter a are harmless: both string parsing and positional accumulation ignore them.

a.i: Translate each letter into its digit character, join them into one string, and hand the result to the language's integer parser, which silently drops the leading zero of letter a. This is the most literal transcription of the statement and hard to get wrong.
s: Build the digit string by replacing each letter with its 0-9 digit character.
Parse each of the three digit strings into an integer.
Return whether first + second equals target.
a.t: O(L) — one pass per word to build digits plus linear parsing.

a.i: Skip strings entirely: fold letters left to right with v = v * 10 + (letter - 'a'). Each letter contributes its face value shifted by the number of remaining letters, which reproduces decimal place values exactly. Constant auxiliary space and marginally faster in practice.
s: For each letter update v = v * 10 + (c - 'a').
Apply to all three words and compare first + second with target.
a.t: O(L) — a single scan per word.

w: Either approach passes instantly; prefer Horner accumulation since it avoids allocations and mirrors hand parsing. Pitfalls: the offset is c - 'a' (not +1), and although values fit easily in 32 bits given length <= 8, widening to 64-bit costs nothing. Follow-up: if letters exceeded j or words grew long, you would reach for big integers or modular arithmetic.
